bib.title: From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Co-Evolution Governance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Co-Evolution Governance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents" (MSCE), Bo Tang, Yang Zhang, Guomian Zhuang et al. (MemTensor, USTC, PolyU et al.). arXiv 2607.16621v1 [cs.CL], 18 Jul 2026 (dated 21 Jul 2026). Preprint, no venue. Code: MemTensor/MemOS.

COVERAGE: 85,779 of 85,779 chars read, including main text, limitations, references, appendices A-E (prompts). Extraction was clean. I did not run the figures script (the Fig. 2 and 3 values came through as text).

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Hierarchical memory plus skills beats flat retrieval of past experience by a wide margin. This is the claim closest to the chapter's raw trajectories vs skills question.
 number: Flat Memory drops Pass@1 by 15.38 (IR), 16.00 (Math), 19.23 (SE) points vs full MSCE.
 setup: EvoAgentBench, GPT-5.2 backbone, OpenClaw runtime; Flat Memory = one non-hierarchical store retrieved directly, with no gating and no skills. Single run, small per-domain task counts (the Pass@1 values are multiples of ~1/26 to 1/78).
 quote: "The largest degradation comes from replacing MSCE with Flat Memory : Pass@1 drops by 15.38, 16.00, and 19.23 points on IR, Math, and SE, respectively"
 where: Sec 5.4, p.10 (Table 3)
2. Crystallizing policies into skills is the most consistent single component. Removing it costs 6.15-11.54 Pass@1 points and raises cost in every domain.
 number: 6.15-11.54 points
 setup: ablation "w/o Skill Crystallization" (policies stay as memory, not callable skills), same benchmark
 quote: "removing skill crystallization causes the most consistent degradation, re-ducing Pass@1 by 6.15–11.54 points across domains and increasing cost for every domain."
 where: Sec 5.4, p.10
3. MSCE beats the memory-only and trajectory-to-skill baselines on EvoAgentBench.
 number: IR 26.15 vs 21.54 (EverOS); Math 47.00 vs 43.00 (EverOS); SE 53.85 vs 38.46 (vanilla/Memento/MemSkill); Code 61.54 (tied with EvoSkill, 2.0 vs 3.9 turns); KW 53.45 vs 48.28. Vanilla agent: IR 12.31, Math 30.00, SE 38.46, Code 51.28, KW 44.83.
 setup: Pass@1 %, all methods on identical runtime, tools, budgets and task order; GPT-5.2 agent, GPT-4o for auxiliary operators; memory accumulated online, then reused on later evaluation
 quote: "Compared with the strongest non-MSCE baseline in each domain, it improves Pass@1 by 4.61 points on IR, 4.00 on Math, 15.39 on SE, and 5.17 on KW."
 where: Sec 5.2, Table 1, p.7
 Baselines: Vanilla; memory-based (Memento, EverOS, MemSkill); trajectory-to-skill (EvoSkill, OpenSpace, SkillFlow-Evolve). Note that several baselines score below vanilla in places. For example, EverOS SE 26.92, EvoSkill SE 26.92, OpenSpace KW 31.03 vs vanilla 44.83. So naive memory or skill reuse can hurt.
4. Experience transfers across domains, and gains accumulate over lifelong use.
 number: cross-domain +2.56 to +5.13 points, mean +3.93 across 6 pairs; lifelong gains from p0 to p100 of +17.00 (Math), +15.39 (SE), +13.84 (IR).
 setup: cross = initialise with memory and skills evolved on source domain, then evolve and evaluate on target. p0 = no accumulation; p25/p50/p100 = growing experience. Cost rises at p25 and then falls.
 quote: "cross-domain transfer improves Pass@1 across all six transfer pairs, with gains from +2.56 to +5.13 points and an average gain of +3.93 points"
 where: Sec 5.3, p.8-9 (Fig 2, Fig 3)
5. On long-dialogue memory (LoCoMo), MSCE edges out the best baseline, a skill-evolution method.
 number: overall judge 61.23 vs 59.22 (SkillFlow-Evolve); F1 49.89 vs 48.71; vanilla 24.35 / 25.95.
 setup: LoCoMo, GPT-4o judge
 quote: "MSCE achieves the best overall judge score and F1, outperforming the strongest baseline, SkillFlow-Evolve, by 2.01 and 1.18 points, respectively."
 where: Sec 5.2, Table 2, p.8
6. Value calibration (applicability filtering) matters, because injecting skills without it hurts. Textual feedback from a stronger mentor model improves results further.
 number: w/o Value Calibration lowers Pass@1 and raises cost in every domain, e.g. SE 53.85 to 50.00, KW 53.45 to 50.00. Simulated feedback gives KW +13.79 and SE +7.69, with Math +0.00.
 setup: the feedback mentor is Opus 4.7 Max, injected only during training and removed at eval (App D.2, Table 7)
 quote: "disabling the value calibration lowers Pass@1 and increases cost in every domain, supporting the need for applicability-aware filtering to avoid harmful skill injection."
 where: Sec 5.4 p.10; App D.2 p.21

Method in brief: L1 grounded step traces, L2 procedural policies, L3 declarative environment cognition, and a skill library (trigger, procedure, verification, boundary, evidence anchors, guidance, reliability) downstream of them. A policy needs evidence from at least 2 distinct episodes (nmin=2) and gain above 0 (G > θG, θG=0) to be promoted to a skill. Skills move probationary, then active (reliability η>0.6), then archived (η<0.2). Step values come from reward backfilling, V_t = α_t R + (1−α_t)γ V_{t+1}, where α is an LLM score of how faithful the self-reflection is. Skills are built from governed memory, not distilled straight from raw trajectories, because "Directly distilled skills may thus overfit to raw trajectories and be invoked in inappropriate contexts." (p.2)

LIMITS
- The authors concede that values, gains and reliability are "heuristic governance signals rather than causal credit-assignment estimates".
- Five operators rely on prompted LLMs, which adds noise, latency and cost.
- It depends on one runtime, tool interface and backbone, so absolute results may vary.
- Stored traces could still retain sensitive information or unsafe procedures.
- Not shown: no seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests appear in the tables, though the text says "significantly outperforms". Per-domain test sets are small.
- Not shown: it does not isolate raw trajectories vs insights vs skill files as separate arms. Flat Memory also removes gating and L3, so it confounds several factors.
- Not shown: it does not test whether skills equal in-context history, so it does not directly contradict ContinualSkillBench. The skill-vs-memory gain here comes bundled with a heavy governance pipeline.
- Authors are from MemTensor (MemOS), so the proposed system and its code share a vendor. Several baselines are adapted (SkillFlow-Evolve is "adapted from SkillFlow"). Cost is not comparable across domains, and lower cost may reflect early stopping.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Reflection: Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023), ExpeL (Zhao et al., AAAI 2024), Think-in-Memory (Liu et al., 2023), SAMULE (2025), PreFlect (2026).
- Memory: Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025), HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., NeurIPS 2024), MemoryOS (Kang et al., EMNLP 2025), EverMemOS (Hu et al., 2026), G-Memory, ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2025), Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., ICML 2025).
- Skills: Anthropic Agent Skills (Oct 2025), Voyager (Wang et al., TMLR 2023), EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026), SkillFlow (Zhang et al., 2026), SkillRL (Xia et al., 2026), SkillNet and CUA-Skill (2026), MemSkill and ProcMEM (2026, concurrent).
- Search: LATS (Zhou et al., ICML 2024).
- Benchmarks: EvoAgentBench, LoCoMo (Maharana et al., ACL 2024), BrowseComp-Plus, OmniMath, SWE-Bench, LiveCodeBench, GDPVal.
- Memory taxonomy follows Wang et al. [31] (cited as Memex(RL), 2026).

CODE (verbatim, p.5 and App B.4, B.8)
- Backfill: V(f_{i,t}) = α_{i,t} R_i + (1 − α_{i,t}) γ V(f_{i,t+1})
- Policy gain: G(f(2)) = V̄_with − V̄_blend(S_without); the baseline of 0.5 is shrunk with pseudocount N0=5.
- Skill reliability: η = (n_pass + 1)/(n_trial + 2)
- The worked example in App C gives V = 0.7 × 0.8 + (1 − 0.7) × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.776.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.4): MSCE overview showing the L1/L2/L3 stack, the skill card fields and the lifecycle probationary, active, archived. It is the clearest picture of "trace vs policy vs environment fact vs skill" and is the one candidate. Fig 2 (cross-domain transfer) and Fig 3 (lifelong p0 to p100) are plain bar/line plots whose values are in the claims above.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found. The appendix prompts are the paper's own LLM prompts, not directed at me.
- Minor extraction faults such as ligature spacing and mangled math symbols; no gaps.
- The "significantly" claim has no statistics. The App E prompt contains a stray ", 12 extra entries" (probably "1-2"), which is an extraction artifact.
